title: Federal Pandemic Relief and United States Hospitals: Who Received It, What It Did to Margins and Closures, and What Happened When It Ended, 2011–2023
content: (Objective) To examine the allocation, effects and aftermath of federal pandemic relief to United States hospitals: which facilities and communities received most of it, whether it was followed by fewer closures and by changes in financial position, whether it altered the relationship between financial indicators and closure, and whether it narrowed or widened differences between hospitals serving different communities. (Methods) Using Medicare cost reports for US general acute care and critical access hospitals, 2011–2023, we compared median operating and total margins over time, estimated observed-to-expected closure ratios for 2017–2019 and 2020–2021 using an early-warning model trained on pre-pandemic data, and measured relief intensity as the change in other income as a share of revenue from 2018–2019 to 2020–2021 among 4074 hospitals reporting in every year from 2018 to 2023. Linear models related relief intensity to changes in margins through 2022–2023. (Results) In 2020, the median total margin rose to 7.7% while the median operating margin fell to −5.6%. Closures in 2017–2019 exceeded model predictions (observed ÷ expected 1.26), whereas closures in 2020–2021 were below predictions (0.73; 95% CI 0.53–0.97), including among distressed hospitals. Hospitals with the most relief had the largest pandemic operating losses and, from 2020–2021 to 2022–2023, the largest declines in total margin (median −8.2 points in the top quartile vs −0.9 in the bottom quartile); each percentage point of relief intensity was associated with a 0.46-point larger decline. (Conclusions) Pandemic relief coincided with fewer closures than expected but masked persistent operating losses, leaving the most relief-dependent hospitals facing a financial cliff when relief ended. It also acted as an equaliser while in place: the association between county poverty and hospital margin fell to zero and the gap between critical access and other hospitals reversed, both returning once support stopped.
